query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, molybdenum‐rich surface coating applied to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion by forming a stable, passivating Mo oxide layer that inhibits aluminum attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based components as used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment without any additional surface modifications.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin Mo-rich (molybdenum) interlayer (e.g., via sputtering or physical vapor deposition) on the component surface.
generation.conditions: Components exposed to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (~660 °C) under standard thermal cycling and exposure times used in industrial applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A modified near-surface structure wherein Mo atoms are incorporated into the outer layer, enabling the formation of a continuous Mo oxide barrier.
generation.mechanism: The Mo-rich coating, upon exposure to the high-temperature, molten-aluminum environment, oxidizes to form a protective Mo-oxide layer. This layer acts as a diffusion barrier that limits the attack of molten aluminum on the underlying boride structure, thereby reducing corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated boride components, the Mo-coated components will show a lower corrosion current density and reduced mass loss, indicating an improved molten-aluminum corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Unmodified boride-based components tested under identical molten-Al conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the Mo coating may depend on its thickness, adhesion, and stability; if the coating is too thick, it may suffer from mechanical wear, and if the operating temperature or cyclic conditions exceed the stability range of the Mo-oxide, the protective effect might diminish.
generation.uncertainty: While the passivation benefit of Mo in high-temperature alloys is supported, the precise degree of corrosion reduction in a molten-aluminum environment and long-term durability under service conditions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based component samples: one set to receive a thin Mo-rich coating via sputtering, and a control set with no coating. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at ~660 °C for a predefined period that simulates hot-dip plating conditions. Post-exposure, evaluate the samples for mass loss, surface microstructure, and corrosion current density using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
measurements: Mass loss measurements to determine the extent of material degradation
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) data to quantify corrosion current density
Surface composition analysis (e.g., XPS or EDS) to verify the presence and integrity of the Mo oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion indicators (mass loss and corrosion current density) compared to the control samples, or if the Mo-rich layer does not display the anticipated stable oxide formation under measurement, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that, by reducing the Mn concentration (to 5 at.% Mn), the CoCrFeMnNi alloy acquires higher yield strength values after annealing at 1117 K (from 387 to 477 MPa) due to the grain refinement effect (from 4.4 to 2.61 µm) []. Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. Such alloys have been designed for the manufacture of furnace casings and chemical tanks used in high-temperature and corrosion conditions [], for components used in the geothermal industry [,], or to obtain high-performance coatings [].
